Poland explainer

By: Laura Byrne | Paid

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
After 120 security personnel and journalists spent over 24 hours stranded on the tarmac at Chopin Airport, we ask: was this a diplomatic blunder, or the result of anti-South African prejudice?

Unique Selling Point:
Introducing our live studio guest, former head of security for Nelson Mandela, Rory Steyn, we take a look at what happened to the plane carrying media and security personnel on President Ramaphosa's much-vaunted peace-keeping visit to Russia and Ukraine.

Summary:
On 15 June 2023, an SAA charter flight carrying more than 120 people, reported as members of the Special Forces and Presidential Protection Unit (including specialist security personnel, senior security staff and leadership), and journalists, was detained on the tarmac at Chopin Airport in Warsaw, Poland. According to a statement by the Polish authorities, Poland had not been notified of the arrival of some of those onboard, although the SA Presidency insisted that all passengers had Polish visas.

Poland also claimed that there were dangerous goods on board, for which permits had not been acquired. Photographs showed around 13 containers on the tarmac, and reports claimed that these were filled with weapons. The presidency insisted that the delegation had all necessary paperwork in place. Wally Rhoode also insisted that the team had permits, although some members only had copies of those permits (apparently the originals were already in Poland with the South African attaché).

On the way to Poland, Italy refused permission for the plane to enter its airspace, resulting in it having to fly laps of the Mediterranean. After the debacle, the expectation was that the plane would join Ramaphosa in Russia, but this didn’t happen, possibly due to failure to acquire overflight permissions for countries in between Poland and Russia. Instead, the plane was sent home to South Africa on 18 June. The South Africans had spent over 26 hours stuck in the plane, before disembarking to a hotel. Meanwhile Ramaphosa continued his tour to Kyiv and St Petersburg with a smaller security detail.

Further information:
Ramaphosa reportedly arrived in Warsaw separately aboard the Inkwazi presidential jet, after attending a UN summit in Geneva, Switzerland. He landed at about the same time, and made a courtesy visit to the Polish president, then embarked on the Kyiv leg of the trip without the rest of his security detail. He was variously reported as being under the protection of an advance team which had travelled to Poland two weeks ahead of Ramaphosa; security provided by the host countries; and his close security detail.

According to a 2018 report by the Institute of Race Relations, expenditure allocated in the 2018/2019 national budget for VIP Protection (VIP Protection Services, Presidential Protection Services, Static and Mobile Security and the 21 (VIP) Squadron) amounted to R2.6bn. The report predicted that just the first two years of Ramaphosa’s new administration (2019/2020 and 2020/2021) would cost R5.8bn in VIP Protection.
The same report says that expenditure on VIP protection is shrouded in secrecy: the last report of the Presidential Protection Services budget was in 2005/2006; there was no transparency on how or on what basis flights are chartered for VIP travel; “Protection Services outcomes, as reported in SAPS annual reports, suggest a decline in work, yet, year-on-year, the budget for VIP Protection grows, more often than not at a rate far greater than inflation”. Zuma’s presidency saw expenditure on VIP Protection explode: R4.3bn in nine years under President Mbeki to R18.2bn in ten years under Zuma.
As a matter of perspective (reported by Daily Maverick) for the same mission:
- Zambian President Hakainde Hichilema travelled with 24 officials, of whom about a dozen were security officers.
- Comorian President Azali Assoumani was accompanied by two security officers and four other officials.
- Senegalese President Macky Sall also had about a dozen security guards
- Egyptian Prime Minister Mostafa Madbouly had a substantial security detail, but reportedly smaller than Ramaphosa’s
On the other hand, the US president travels in an “imperial bubble” – some highlights include:
- Secret service agents arriving months ahead of time to clear airspace, map out routes, and identify hospitals and secure locations
- Extensive airspace restrictions: other aircraft may not fly below 18 000 feet within an “inner ring” 10 miles of the presidential plane, or land at airports. They can fly through but not loiter in an “outer ring” of 30 miles.
- The president travels in a motorcade of about 20 vehicles. Motorways are closed along the route
- The president is escorted by Secret Service counter-assault agents and local police.
- In hotels, the whole floor on which the president stays, plus the floor above and the floor below, are booked out
- An identical backup plane accompanies Airforce One on every trip

Script:


VO: The African peace-keeping mission to the Ukraine and Russia last week rapidly devolved into something between a farce and an international diplomatic scandal.

UPSOUND: AMANDA KHOZA: Since we arrived here during the day we haven’t been able to get off the flight.

VO: A plane carrying around 120 South African security personnel and journalists was stranded at Warsaw Chopin Airport in Poland. Forced to remain aboard for over 24 hours, journalists who expected to report on an historic delegation were reduced to tweeting about…
… a game of musical containers…

UPSOUND: Where are they taking the cargo to?
They’re reloading it.

VO: …inflight entertainment…

UPSOUND: …Ek is ‘n loslappie...

VO: …and dwindling food supplies. But underneath the humour, a political fiasco was brewing.

UPSOUND: CAPTAIN MPHO MAMASHELA: The situation of the aircraft is not a problem. The whole issue is about the mission.

VO: Despite Captain Mpho Mamashela’s confidence, it appears the plane was refused entry into Italian airspace en route. And Poland claimed that crucial permits were missing for some of those on board – and for a dozen containers of weapons.

UPSOUND: MAJ GEN WALLY RHOODE: They say we don’t have permits. We have permits. They are delaying us, right, they are putting the life of our president in jeopardy.

VO: In an impromptu press conference, Head of the Presidential Protection Unit, Major General Wally Rhoode, accused Polish authorities of sabotage and racism. As rumours swirled, Presidency spokesperson Vincent Magwenya insisted that, despite this “regrettable” incident, the mission was going well. Meanwhile President Ramaphosa paid a visit to Polish President Andzrej Duda, then continued undeterred to the Ukraine.

UPSOUND: CYRIL RAMAPHOSA: This is indeed a historic mission, in a quest for peace…

VO: Back in Warsaw, the harassed South Africans were finally allowed to disembark. But hopes that they might join the delegation in Russia were soon dashed.

UPSOUND: [PILOT'S VOICE]: Flying time will be around 11 hours to Waterkloof. Your long arduous journey is almost finished.

VO: Instead, after two nights in a Warsaw hotel, the South Africans arrived home on the 18th of June: an anticlimactic end to the debacle.

UPSOUND: JOURNALIST: We’re back!
